Q011645:
## Why iterative work was slow before Spark
In the MapReduce model every job reads its input from distributed storage and writes its result back to it. An algorithm that loops over the same data 30 times therefore pays 30 reads and 30 writes of the full dataset.
## What Spark changes
Spark executors can hold partitions in memory (and spill to local disk when needed). When a DataFrame is marked with `cache()` or `persist()`, the first action materializes its partitions in the executors, and later actions read them from there instead of recomputing from the source.
- Spark still shuffles and spills when needed; memory is an optimization, not a requirement.
- The same engine also pipelines narrow transformations inside one stage, which saves intermediate writes within a pass.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Lossy compression:** Spark never alters data with a lossy codec. Compression such as Snappy or Zstandard is lossless and does not change how many times the data has to be re-read.
- ✗ **B. Single task for all passes:** each action triggers its own job and the passes depend on earlier results, so Spark cannot merge them into one scan. It reuses cached data rather than skipping the passes.
- ✗ **C. Built-in scheduler:** Spark still uses a cluster manager (standalone, YARN or Kubernetes) to get executors, and negotiation happens once per application, not before each pass. It is not what removes the repeated I/O.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Caching the working dataset in executor memory is the iterative-workload advantage: after the first pass the partitions are served from the executors, so passes 2 to 30 avoid re-reading and re-writing storage.

## Key idea
Spark's iterative speed-up comes from keeping the working set in executor memory between actions instead of round-tripping through storage.
Q011646:
## The unified engine idea
Spark is one engine with several modules on top: Spark SQL and DataFrames, Structured Streaming, MLlib and the pandas API on Spark. They share the same execution core, the Catalyst optimizer for DataFrame and SQL work, and the same cluster resources.
## What that buys a team
- Code for batch and streaming can use the same DataFrame operations, so a transformation written once can serve both.
- One deployment, one security model and one monitoring surface instead of three.
- Data moves between stages of a pipeline (for example ETL output into model training) in the same process rather than across systems.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Own file system:** Spark has no storage layer. It reads and writes external systems such as cloud object storage, HDFS or Delta tables.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** One engine and shared APIs across SQL, streaming and ML is the documented advantage: the same optimizer, scheduler and cluster serve every workload, which removes the three-system fragmentation.
- ✗ **C. Single-node rewrite:** Spark is a distributed engine and does not collapse a pipeline onto one node; its value is scaling out across executors.
- ✗ **D. Automatic conversion to SQL:** each module keeps its own API (for example `readStream` and `pyspark.ml`); they interoperate on DataFrames but are not translated into SQL for you.

## Key idea
Spark's advantage is a unified engine: one set of DataFrame/SQL APIs and one optimizer across batch, streaming and ML.
Q011647:
## Small files and distributed engines
Spark plans file reads by packing files into partitions. `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` (default 128 MB) caps the bytes per partition, and `spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes` (default 4 MB) adds an estimated cost for each file opened. Millions of 50 KB files still need millions of listing calls, open calls and metadata reads, even when Spark packs several files into one partition.
## Why the cluster idles
Per-file overhead is spent mostly on the driver (listing and planning) and in object-store requests, not in CPU on the executors. That is why cores sit idle while the stage is slow.
## What developers do about it
Compact the data into fewer, larger files (for example 128 MB to 1 GB each) when it is written, and avoid writing one file per tiny batch.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Too many executors:** executors do not rebalance cached blocks among themselves because of a read, and the stage in question is a file scan, not a caching problem.
- ✗ **B. Lazy recomputation:** Spark builds the plan once per action, and a folder listing is not repeated per column. The symptom is tied to the file count.
- ✓ **C. This is the small-files challenge (correct):** file open, listing and metadata cost grows with the file count, not the byte count, so 3 million tiny files make the read slow while cores wait.
- ✗ **D. Shuffle cost:** the slow part is the read stage, which has no shuffle yet. A shuffle would show up as shuffle read/write between stages.

## Key idea
Many tiny files make reads slow because per-file overhead dominates; the fix is compaction into fewer, larger files.
Q011648:
## Lineage as fault tolerance
Transformations are lazy: Spark first builds a plan (the lineage) that says how each partition is derived from its inputs. If an executor dies and its partitions or shuffle output are lost, the scheduler re-runs the tasks that produce just those partitions on other executors.
- No replication is needed by default; replicated storage levels such as `MEMORY_ONLY_2` are an opt-in.
- Checkpointing is also opt-in. It truncates long lineages by saving data to reliable storage, but Spark does not do it after every step.
## Limits
The driver must stay alive. Recomputation is cheap for narrow dependencies and costs more when lost output came from a wide (shuffle) dependency.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Lineage-based recomputation is the built-in fault tolerance (correct):** the driver knows how every partition was derived, so only the lost partitions are rebuilt on healthy executors and the job continues.
- ✗ **B. Checkpoint after each step:** checkpointing is explicit (`checkpoint()`), is not automatic, and would be very slow if done after every transformation.
- ✗ **C. Pause and replay on the same node:** the scheduler reschedules the failed tasks on other available executors rather than waiting for the failed node.
- ✗ **D. Automatic 3x replication:** Spark does not replicate partitions by default; replication happens only if you choose a `_2` storage level, and it is not applied before transformations.

## Key idea
Spark tolerates failures by recomputing lost partitions from their lineage on other executors, not by default replication or checkpointing.
Q011649:
## Narrow and wide dependencies
- A **narrow** transformation (`filter`, `select`, `withColumn`, `map`-like) computes each output partition from one input partition. It runs inside the executor that already holds the data and needs no data movement.
- A **wide** transformation (`groupBy`, `join` without broadcast, `orderBy`, `distinct`, `repartition`) needs rows with the same key, or the same sort range, in the same partition. Spark must move rows between executors: map tasks write shuffle files to local disk, and reduce tasks fetch them over the network.
## Why this is the classic Spark cost
Shuffle involves serialization, disk writes and network transfer, and it also marks a stage boundary. Reducing shuffles (filter early, avoid unnecessary sorts, broadcast small tables) is the main performance work in Spark.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Wide transformations such as `orderBy` and `groupBy` shuffle data between executors via disk and network, which is why shuffle read/write dominates the UI and the stages are slower than a narrow `filter`.
- ✗ **B. Narrow slower than wide:** filtering runs in parallel on executors, not on the driver, and needs no data movement, so it is cheaper than a shuffle.
- ✗ **C. Collecting to the driver:** shuffles move data directly between executors. The driver coordinates but does not receive or redistribute the 2 TB.
- ✗ **D. Columnar format blocks parallelism:** formats such as Parquet are columnar and still split into many partitions that run in parallel; the cost here is the shuffle.

## Key idea
The main distributed-processing challenge is shuffle cost: wide transformations move data across the network and through disk, narrow ones do not.
Q011650:
## Distributed data, one driver
A DataFrame is split into partitions stored and processed on many executors, so its total size can be far larger than any one machine. Actions such as `collect()` and `toPandas()` bring rows back to the driver, a single process whose heap is set with `spark.driver.memory`.
## What stops you
`spark.driver.maxResultSize` (default 1 GB) limits the total size of serialized results per action; a job whose results exceed it is aborted. Even below that limit, the deserialized objects can exhaust the driver heap.
## What to do instead
Aggregate or filter on the executors first, write the result to storage, or bound the result with `limit(n)` or `take(n)` for samples.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Full `collect()`:** it returns every row in one list on the driver, not in batches, so 90 GB fails with a driver out-of-memory error or a `spark.driver.maxResultSize` error.
- ✗ **B. `rdd.collect()`:** it is the same action on the same data and returns the whole dataset to the driver at once; nothing is streamed or released.
- ✗ **C. `toPandas()` without a limit:** it also collects all rows into one pandas DataFrame on the driver; Arrow only speeds up the transfer and does not shrink the data.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** `limit(20)` makes Spark compute at most 20 rows, so `collect()` returns only those rows to the driver; the other calls try to move all 90 GB into one process.

## Key idea
Actions that return data (`collect`, `toPandas`) move distributed data into a single driver, so bound the result with `limit` or aggregate on executors.
Q011651:
## Structured APIs versus Python lambdas
A DataFrame or SQL query describes what you want. Spark parses it into a logical plan, the Catalyst optimizer improves it (column pruning, predicate pushdown, join strategy), and the JVM executes the optimized plan on executors. In PySpark the Python code only builds the plan, so a built-in expression such as `F.sum` runs at JVM speed for every language.
## What the lambda version pays
`df.rdd.map(lambda ...)` hands rows to Python worker processes: each row is serialized from the JVM to Python and back, and Catalyst cannot see inside the lambda to optimize it. This is the main reason structured APIs and built-in functions are preferred.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Global interpreter lock across the cluster:** the lock applies per Python process, not to the whole cluster. The RDD job still runs in parallel across workers, just with per-row serialization cost.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The DataFrame version is planned by Catalyst and executed inside the JVM, so no Python call is made per row; the RDD lambda version serializes rows to Python workers and gets no optimization.
- ✗ **C. Everything on disk:** DataFrames use memory and spill to disk when needed. Being on disk is not the reason, and it would normally be slower.
- ✗ **D. Runs only on the driver:** DataFrame work is distributed across executors like any other Spark job; the driver builds the plan and coordinates.

## Key idea
Structured APIs let Catalyst optimize and run the work in the JVM, so they beat Python lambdas that serialize each row.
Q011652:
## The three roles in a Spark application
- The **driver** runs your main program (it hosts the `SparkSession` and `SparkContext`). It builds the plan for every action, divides it into stages and tasks, and schedules them on executors. It also collects the results of actions.
- The **cluster manager** (standalone, YARN or Kubernetes) only allocates resources: it launches executors for the application. It does not read your code.
- **Executors** are processes on worker nodes that run tasks and hold cached data. Each application gets its own executors.
## Consequence
The driver must be reachable from the executors for the whole lifetime of the application, and it should run close to the workers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cluster manager:** it hands out resources (containers or pods for executors), but it does not understand the application's DataFrame code or create stages.
- ✗ **B. Executors negotiating:** executors run the tasks they receive and report back to the driver. They do not plan stages or coordinate with each other to share jobs.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** The driver turns DataFrame operations into a plan, divides it into stages and tasks, and ships the tasks to executors; this is the scheduling role of the driver program.
- ✗ **D. Worker OS:** the operating system only schedules processes and threads. Spark's own DAG and task schedulers in the driver decide what tasks exist.

## Key idea
The driver plans and schedules; the cluster manager allocates executors; executors run tasks and cache data.
Q011653:
## Resource negotiation
When an application starts, its SparkContext connects to a cluster manager (Spark's standalone manager, Hadoop YARN or Kubernetes). The application requests executors with settings such as `spark.executor.instances`, `spark.executor.cores` and `spark.executor.memory`, and the manager decides whether it can grant them and where to run them.
## Spark's stance
Spark is agnostic to the manager: once it has executors that can talk to each other and to the driver, it works the same way. The cluster manager also divides resources among different applications on the cluster, while scheduling inside one application is done by Spark itself.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Block manager:** it stores and serves data blocks (cached partitions, shuffle output). It does not allocate other executors' memory or processes.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The cluster manager allocates executors across applications and launches them with the requested cores and memory; Spark is agnostic about which manager is used.
- ✗ **C. SQL catalog:** it holds metadata about databases, tables and functions. Resource sizing is a configuration of the application and the cluster manager, not catalog metadata.
- ✗ **D. Driver task scheduler:** it assigns tasks to executor slots that already exist. It does not create executor processes or decide their size.

## Key idea
The cluster manager hands out executors (cores and memory); the driver schedules tasks onto them.
Q011654:
## Unified memory
Executor heap use in Spark falls into execution memory (shuffles, joins, sorts, aggregations) and storage memory (cached data, broadcast data). They share one unified region M.
- `spark.memory.fraction` (default 0.6) sets the size of M as a fraction of the heap minus about 300 MiB. The remaining 40% is for user data structures, internal metadata and a safety margin against out-of-memory errors.
- `spark.memory.storageFraction` (default 0.5) sets the size of the subregion R inside M where cached blocks are never evicted by execution.
## Borrowing rules
When no execution memory is in use, storage may take all of M and the other way around. Execution can evict cached blocks, but only until storage falls to R. Storage cannot evict execution memory. Most users should leave both settings at their defaults.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. `spark.executor.memoryOverhead`:** this is non-heap memory for VM and native overhead; it is not the cache protection setting.
- ✗ **B. `spark.memory.fraction`:** it sizes the whole unified region M (default 0.6 of heap), within which execution may still evict cache above R.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** `spark.memory.storageFraction` sets R, the part of the unified region in which cached blocks are immune to eviction by execution.
- ✗ **D. `spark.driver.maxResultSize`:** it caps serialized action results returned to the driver and has nothing to do with executor storage.

## Key idea
`spark.memory.fraction` sizes unified memory M; `spark.memory.storageFraction` sizes the eviction-protected cache part R inside it.
Q011655:
## Cores are task slots
Each executor runs tasks in parallel in threads, one task per core when `spark.task.cpus` is 1. The total number of tasks that can run at the same time is `executors x cores per executor`. Here that is `3 x 4 = 12` slots.
## Waves
If a stage has more tasks than slots, the extra tasks queue and run as slots free up. With 60 equal tasks and 12 slots, `60 / 12 = 5` waves of 10 seconds each, so about 50 seconds.
- Fewer partitions than slots leaves cores idle.
- Many more partitions than slots is fine and helps balance uneven tasks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** The cluster has 12 task slots, so 60 equal tasks of 10 seconds finish in 5 waves, about 50 seconds.
- ✗ **B. All 60 at once:** Spark can run only as many tasks as there are free slots (12); the rest wait.
- ✗ **C. Sequential tasks:** tasks in a stage are independent and run in parallel across all available slots. Stages depend on each other, tasks inside one do not.
- ✗ **D. Only one executor works:** all three executors take tasks at the same time; the 4-core count applies to each executor, so the real slot count is 12, not 4.

## Key idea
Parallel tasks = executors x cores per executor (divided by `spark.task.cpus`); more tasks than slots run in waves.
Q011656:
## What an executor holds
An executor is a process on a worker node. It runs tasks and keeps data blocks for the application: cached partitions in storage memory and shuffle files on local disk. Losing the process loses those blocks and any running tasks.
## What Spark does
The driver detects the lost executor, reschedules the tasks that were running there on the remaining (or newly requested) executors, and recomputes missing cached partitions from the lineage the next time they are needed. If shuffle files were lost, the map tasks that wrote them are re-run. The application survives as long as the driver does.
- Replicated storage levels (`_2`) can reduce recomputation but are opt-in.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Restart everything:** Spark re-runs only the affected tasks and missing partitions or shuffle outputs, not completed work in unaffected partitions.
- ✗ **B. Hidden replica:** there is no replica unless a replicated storage level was chosen, and the cluster manager does not manage data blocks.
- ✗ **C. Application fails:** lost cached blocks are never fatal on their own, because Spark can recompute them. Failure would come from a lost driver or repeated task failures.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** The driver reschedules the failed tasks on other executors and recomputes only the lost cached partitions from lineage when needed, so the application continues.

## Key idea
A lost executor costs recomputation of its partitions from lineage; only losing the driver ends the application.
Q011657:
## Isolation between applications
Each Spark application (one `SparkContext`) gets its own executor processes for the application's whole lifetime. Executors of different applications run in different JVMs, so one application cannot read another's cached blocks, broadcast variables or temporary views.
- Benefits: scheduling and executor isolation between applications.
- Cost: sharing data across applications requires writing it to an external storage system (for example Parquet or Delta files) or a table.
## Within one application
A second `SparkSession` created with `newSession()` shares the `SparkContext` and the table cache, but separate applications do not.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Executors belong to a single application, so cached blocks are private to it; the second notebook reads the table from storage again.
- ✗ **B. Broadcast to attach:** a broadcast variable is a read-only value shipped to one application's executors; it does not expose cached DataFrames to other applications.
- ✗ **C. Same appName:** names are labels for the UI and have no effect on data sharing.
- ✗ **D. Shared block store:** there is no cluster-wide block store across applications; each executor's block manager serves only its own application.

## Key idea
Cached data lives in an application's own executors; separate applications share data only through external storage.
Q011658:
## Which code runs where
- Plain Python statements in your script, such as the `sum` over `rows` and the first `print`, run in the **driver**'s Python process.
- Functions passed to DataFrame or RDD operations (`foreach`, `map`, UDFs) are serialized and sent to the **executors**, where they run on the partitions. Their `print` writes to the executor's stdout, which you can read in the executor logs in the Spark UI.
## Practical rules
- Do not use `foreach` with `print` to see results; use `show()`, `take()` or collect a small sample.
- Do not try to update a driver-side Python variable from inside `foreach`; the closure is copied to executors. An accumulator is the supported way to count things.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cluster manager and driver:** the cluster manager never runs application code, and a `foreach` lambda executes on executors, not on the driver.
- ✗ **B. Both on executors:** the `sum` and first `print` work on a local list in the driver; Spark never forwards executor stdout to the driver console.
- ✗ **C. Both on the driver:** only the driver code runs there. The lambda is executed by tasks on executors, and nothing buffers its output for the driver.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Code outside the Spark operations runs on the driver after `collect` returns, while the `foreach` lambda is shipped to the executors, so its output lands in executor logs.

## Key idea
Top-level Python runs on the driver; lambdas passed to DataFrame operations run on the executors, so their output goes to executor logs.
Q011659:
## DataFrame and Dataset
- A **DataFrame** is a distributed collection of rows organized into named columns, like a table. It carries a schema, so Spark can optimize queries over it.
- A **Dataset** adds compile-time types in Scala and Java (`Dataset[T]`); a DataFrame is `Dataset[Row]` there.
- **Python has no Dataset API.** PySpark developers use the DataFrame; column types are checked at analysis time (when the query is resolved), not at compile time.
## Same engine
DataFrame and SQL operations are planned by Catalyst and executed by the same JVM engine regardless of language, so PySpark DataFrame code gets the same optimizations as Scala.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Different engine:** the DataFrame in Python builds the same logical plan; the plan then runs in the JVM, so optimizations match.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The typed Dataset exists only for Scala and Java; PySpark's DataFrame uses the same Catalyst optimizer and execution engine.
- ✗ **C. Decorator for typed Dataset:** PySpark has no typed Dataset, and Python's dynamic typing means schema errors are caught when the query is analyzed, not compiled.
- ✗ **D. Only RDDs:** DataFrames are fully supported in PySpark and are the recommended API; RDDs are the low-level alternative.

## Key idea
PySpark has DataFrames only (typed Datasets are Scala/Java), and both share the Catalyst engine.
Q011660:
## SparkSession lifecycle
`SparkSession` is the entry point to DataFrame and SQL functionality. In a notebook or `pyspark` shell the platform usually creates `spark` for you.
- `builder.getOrCreate()` first checks for a valid global default session. If one exists it is returned (builder options are applied to it); otherwise a new session is built and becomes the default.
- A JVM hosts one active `SparkContext` per application, so extra calls do not add executors.
- `spark.newSession()` creates a session with separate SQL configuration, temporary views and UDFs but the same `SparkContext` and table cache.
- `spark.stop()` ends the session and the context, releasing executors.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Second context:** one application runs one `SparkContext`; calling the builder again does not start more executors.
- ✗ **B. Error on second build:** the builder is designed to be called repeatedly; nothing raises just because a session exists.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** `getOrCreate()` returns the existing global default session if there is one, so the second call reuses it rather than creating another context.
- ✗ **D. Stop and rebuild:** `getOrCreate()` never stops a running session; only `spark.stop()` does that.

## Key idea
`getOrCreate()` is idempotent: it returns the active session and does not create a second context.
Q011661:
## Caching is lazy
`cache()` is shorthand for `persist()` with the default storage level. It does not run a job. It tells Spark to keep the partitions of this DataFrame's plan once they are computed.
- The first action (here `count()`) computes the partitions and stores them in executor storage memory.
- Later actions on the same cached plan read the stored partitions instead of re-reading Parquet and re-applying the filter.
## Default level
For DataFrames the default is `MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER`, so partitions that do not fit in memory spill to local disk rather than being dropped. `unpersist()` frees the blocks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. RDD-only:** DataFrames have `cache()` and `persist()` and use the same block storage; the effect is documented for DataFrames.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** `cache()` marks the DataFrame; the first action `count()` fills the cache, and the second action reads the cached partitions instead of rescanning Parquet.
- ✗ **C. Immediate load:** `cache()` is lazy and runs nothing, so the first action still has to read the files once.
- ✗ **D. Per-action lifetime:** cached blocks stay in executors until `unpersist()`, eviction or the end of the application, so later actions reuse them.

## Key idea
`cache()` is lazy: the first action populates it and later actions read from it.
Q011662:
## Storage levels and what happens when memory is short
The `StorageLevel` decides where cached partitions live:
- `MEMORY_ONLY`: partitions that do not fit in memory are not cached and are recomputed each time they are needed.
- `MEMORY_AND_DISK`: partitions that do not fit in memory are stored on local disk and read from there.
- `DISK_ONLY`: partitions are only on disk.
- `_2` variants (for example `MEMORY_AND_DISK_2`) replicate each partition on two nodes.
For RDDs in PySpark, stored objects are always serialized with Pickle, so a serialized level makes no difference there; DataFrames are cached by the JVM.
## Choosing
Use the default memory-first level when data fits. When recomputation is expensive, as with a slow JDBC read, spill to disk (a local disk read is much cheaper than a database round trip).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. `MEMORY_ONLY`:** with only 10 GB of storage for 25 GB of data, most partitions would be recomputed from the database on every action, which is the cost to avoid.
- ✗ **B. `DISK_ONLY`:** it wastes the memory that could hold part of the data and makes every read slower than needed.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** `MEMORY_AND_DISK` keeps what fits in memory and spills the rest to local disk, so the slow JDBC source is not queried again for the overflow.
- ✗ **D. `MEMORY_AND_DISK_2`:** replication doubles the storage needed and addresses node loss, not a shortage of memory; it is not the only way to keep the data complete.

## Key idea
When recomputation is expensive and memory is short, use `MEMORY_AND_DISK` so overflow spills to disk instead of being recomputed.
Q011663:
## What fills storage memory
Cached blocks stay in executor storage memory until `unpersist()` is called, they are evicted (least recently used) to make room, or the application ends. A loop that caches a new DataFrame each time and never releases the old ones accumulates dead blocks. Spark eventually evicts them, but only under pressure, which shows up as slow stages and recomputation.
## The fix
`df.unpersist()` marks the DataFrame as non-persistent and removes all its blocks from memory and disk. Unpersist an old result after the next one has been computed (so you do not drop data you still need).
- `spark.catalog.clearCache()` removes every cached table and DataFrame in the session, including ones you still need.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Calling `cache()` again:** marking an already cached plan changes nothing and gives no priority; old blocks stay until evicted.
- ✗ **B. `clearCache()` every iteration:** it drops all cached data in the session, including tables still needed later, causing recomputation.
- ✗ **C. `checkpoint()`:** it writes the data to reliable storage and truncates lineage, but it does not remove other DataFrames' cached blocks.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** `unpersist()` on the previous iteration's DataFrame releases exactly the blocks that are no longer needed, keeping storage memory free for the current iteration.

## Key idea
Release cached DataFrames you no longer need with `unpersist()`; otherwise they hold storage memory until evicted.
Q011664:
## GC cost in Spark
Garbage collection cost grows with the number of Java objects. Caching many objects on the JVM heap fills the Old (tenured) generation, and full collections then pause tasks.
## Tuning guide steps
- Measure first: add verbose GC options and look at how often collections run and how long they take (the logs are on the worker nodes).
- If the Old generation is close to full, **lower `spark.memory.fraction`** (default 0.6) so that less memory is used for caching; the guide says it is better to cache fewer objects than to slow down tasks.
- Alternatively reduce the Young generation size, and consider storing data in a compact (serialized) form to cut the object count.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Lowering `spark.memory.fraction` reduces how much the heap is used for cached objects, which relieves a nearly full Old generation; the tuning guide lists this as the step for this symptom.
- ✗ **B. Replication:** a `_2` level stores a second copy on another node, which adds memory pressure instead of removing it.
- ✗ **C. Raising the fraction:** it lets Spark use even more of the heap for cache and execution, which makes a full Old generation worse.
- ✗ **D. More shuffle partitions:** this changes task sizes in shuffle stages but does not reduce the objects held in the Old generation by cached data.

## Key idea
When GC logs show a nearly full Old generation, cache fewer objects (lower `spark.memory.fraction`) or store data more compactly.
Q011665:
## What a session owns
A `SparkSession` keeps its own SQL configuration, registered temporary views and UDFs. `newSession()` creates another session that shares only the underlying `SparkContext` (so the same executors) and the table cache.
- `createOrReplaceTempView` registers a view in the current session only. The other session does not see it.
- A global temporary view (`createGlobalTempView`) is shared across sessions of one application under the `global_temp` database.
## Why it matters
Sessions give isolation of SQL settings and temporary names inside one application without paying for new executors.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. New application:** the new session shares the same SparkContext and executors, so it is not a new application; the failure is about the view name scope.
- ✗ **B. Copied views:** `newSession()` starts with separate SQLConf, views and UDFs, not a copy of the creator's registered views.
- ✗ **C. Shared views:** views are per session; sharing across sessions would need a global temporary view.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Temporary views are scoped to the session that registered them, so the new session fails to find `t` even though both sessions share one SparkContext.

## Key idea
Temporary views are session-scoped; `newSession()` shares the SparkContext and cache but not views, UDFs or SQL settings.
Q011666:
## Action starts a job
Spark's hierarchy begins with the **job**: a parallel computation spawned in response to an action such as `count`, `collect` or `save`/`write`. Transformations (`range`, `filter`, `withColumn`, `select`, `join`) are lazy: they extend the logical plan and nothing runs.
- The `count()` line triggers one job that computes the result for the driver.
- The `write` line triggers another job that writes the output files.
Each job is then split into stages and tasks. Both jobs recompute `df`, `a` and `b` because nothing was cached.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Only actions create jobs, so `count()` and `write` each start one, while `range`, `filter` and `withColumn` just build the plan.
- ✗ **B. Only write:** `count()` is an action that has to compute the number of rows from a non-trivial plan (filter and withColumn), so it runs a job.
- ✗ **C. Every line:** creating a DataFrame from a transformation does not compute anything; execution waits for an action.
- ✗ **D. Transformations run first:** it is the opposite; transformations are lazy and actions trigger execution.

## Key idea
A job is created per action; transformations only extend the plan.
Q011667:
## Stages are cut at shuffles
Spark divides a job into **stages** at shuffle boundaries. Within a stage, narrow transformations are pipelined: each task runs `filter`, `withColumn` and similar operations on its partition in a single pass without moving data.
- Narrow: `filter`, `select`, `withColumn`, `union`, and `coalesce` (it merges existing partitions on the same executor where possible, with no full shuffle by default).
- Wide: `groupBy` aggregations, most joins, `distinct`, `orderBy`, `repartition`.
## In this pipeline
Before the `groupBy`, one stage reads, filters, adds the column and coalesces. The `groupBy` introduces the shuffle: a second stage reads shuffle output and counts per key.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. `filter`:** it works on each row independently inside its partition, so no data moves.
- ✗ **B. `withColumn`:** computing a column is a per-row, per-partition operation; other partitions do not need the value.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** `groupBy("k").count()` needs all rows of a key together, so a shuffle (and a stage boundary) is required; the earlier steps are narrow and pipelined into the first stage.
- ✗ **D. `coalesce(4)`:** it narrows partitions by combining existing ones without a full shuffle (unlike `repartition`), so it does not create a stage boundary by default.

## Key idea
A shuffle (wide dependency) such as `groupBy` ends a stage; narrow steps are pipelined inside one.
Q011668:
## Tasks and partitions
A **task** is the unit of work sent to an executor: one task processes one partition of the stage's input. The number of tasks in a stage therefore equals the number of partitions of the data it reads.
- Narrow operations (`filter`, `select`) do not change the partition count, so the first stage has 8 tasks.
- `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (default 200) sets the partition count after a shuffle, which affects the stage that reads shuffle output (and AQE can coalesce it), not the first stage reading source data.
## Consequence
Parallelism is limited by the number of partitions and the number of executor cores that can run the tasks at the same time.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One per row:** tasks work on whole partitions of many rows each, not on single rows.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The first stage reads the 8 partitions of the range, so it runs 8 tasks, one per partition; `filter` and `select` keep the partitioning.
- ✗ **C. One per job:** a job has many tasks; a stage runs a task per partition.
- ✗ **D. 200 per stage:** the shuffle partition setting applies to stages that read shuffle output, not to the stage reading the source.

## Key idea
Number of tasks in a stage = number of partitions it processes.
Q011669:
## Task failure handling
Tasks are the retryable unit. When a task fails, the task scheduler retries it, often on a different executor (for example if the executor itself is unhealthy). The setting `spark.task.maxFailures` (default 4) is the number of failures of any particular task before the job is given up.
- Completed tasks of the stage keep their output.
- A failed job is reported with the cause of the last failure; the usual causes are deterministic errors (bad data, code exceptions, out of memory) that fail every retry.
## Why this matters
A transient problem is absorbed by retries, while a repeating error shows up as a failed job and stage in the UI.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Immediate abort:** a single failure of a task is expected in a large cluster and is retried first.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Spark retries the failed task (possibly elsewhere) up to `spark.task.maxFailures` times, and the job is aborted only if that limit is hit.
- ✗ **C. Rerun the entire stage:** only the failed task is rescheduled; successful tasks keep their results.
- ✗ **D. Skip the partition:** Spark never silently drops data; a task that keeps failing fails the job.

## Key idea
Tasks are retried individually (default 4 attempts); only repeated failure of one task aborts the job.
Q011670:
## Where skipped stages come from
When a job has a shuffle, the map-side tasks write shuffle files to the executors' local disk and the next stage reads them. If another job in the same application reuses the same shuffled data (same plan, shuffle files still present), the scheduler does not re-run the map stage and the UI marks it **skipped**.
- Skipped does not mean failed or cancelled; the work was done earlier.
- This is separate from `cache()`. It relies on the shuffle files remaining on executors, and it ends if those executors are lost.
## Hierarchy recap
Application -> jobs (one per action) -> stages (cut at shuffles) -> tasks (one per partition).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Replicated tasks:** tasks are not replicated automatically; a stage is skipped because its output already exists.
- ✗ **B. Cancelled job:** the second job runs and produces output; skipped refers to one stage inside a successful job.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Shuffle files from the first job are still on the executors, so the second job reuses that map-side output and shows the stage as skipped.
- ✗ **D. AQE removed the stage:** AQE re-optimizes plans from runtime statistics but does not skip a stage merely because of an empty result, and the cause here is reuse of shuffle files.

## Key idea
A skipped stage means its shuffle output from an earlier job was reused instead of recomputed.
Q011671:
## The execution hierarchy
- A **task** is the unit of work sent to one executor; it processes one partition.
- A **stage** is a set of tasks that can run the same code in parallel on different partitions, with stage boundaries at shuffles.
- A **job** is created by an action and consists of one or more stages that depend on each other.
- An **application** is one `SparkContext` (a driver and its executors) and runs many jobs over its lifetime.
## Reading the Spark UI
The Jobs tab lists jobs, each job page lists its stages, and each stage page lists its tasks with durations and metrics.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** A task is part of a stage, a stage is part of a job, and a job is part of an application, so smallest to largest is task, stage, job, application.
- ✗ **B. Job before stage:** a job is made of stages and so is larger than a stage; an application is larger than both but the first three are in the wrong order.
- ✗ **C. Job before stage:** a job is the larger container of stages, so it must come after stage and not before it.
- ✗ **D. Stage before task:** a stage consists of tasks, so a task is the smaller unit.

## Key idea
Application contains jobs, jobs contain stages, stages contain tasks.
Q011672:
## Run SQL on files directly
Spark SQL can query a file without a read call or a view. The table identifier is the data source name, a dot, and the path in backticks:
- `SELECT * FROM parquet.`/data/users.parquet``
- `SELECT * FROM json.`/data/events``
The source name before the dot (`parquet`, `json`, `csv`, `orc`, `text`) tells Spark which reader to use, and the backticks mark the path as one identifier. `spark.sql(...)` returns a normal DataFrame, so you can keep transforming it.
## What this form does not give you
The files are read with the default options of that source. If you need options such as a header, a delimiter or an explicit schema, use `spark.read.option(...).schema(...)` instead.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. USING clause:** `USING json` belongs to `CREATE TABLE` and `CREATE TEMPORARY VIEW` statements; it is not valid inside a plain SELECT, so the query fails to parse.
- ✗ **B. Single quotes:** a quoted string is a literal, not an identifier. The path has to sit in backticks after the source name, so this statement is a syntax error.
- ✗ **C. file() function:** Spark SQL has no table function with this name for reading paths. Direct file queries use the `source.`path`` identifier.
- ✓ **D. Source name plus backticked path (correct):** `json.` followed by the path in backticks is the documented "run SQL on files directly" form, and the result is a DataFrame.

## Key idea
Query a file in place with `SELECT ... FROM format.`path``; backticks, not quotes, and default reader options only.
Q011673:
## Save modes
`DataFrameWriter.mode()` tells Spark what to do when the target already holds data. The four modes:
- `errorifexists` (also `error`, the default): throw an exception if data exists.
- `append`: add the DataFrame's rows to the existing data.
- `overwrite`: replace the existing data with the DataFrame.
- `ignore`: do nothing if data exists, like `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`.
## Why the default matters
A script that works the first time and fails the second is the signature of the default mode. Nothing is written by the failing call, so the old output is still there.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Overwrite:** overwriting also needs `mode("overwrite")`. Replacing data without being asked would be dangerous, which is why the default refuses.
- ✗ **B. Append:** appending needs an explicit `mode("append")`; it is not the default, and a silent append would duplicate rows on every rerun.
- ✓ **C. Default errorifexists (correct):** with no `mode()` call the writer uses `errorifexists`, so the second write sees data at `/out/daily` and throws an exception before changing anything.
- ✗ **D. Ignore:** skipping an existing target is what `mode("ignore")` does. The default does not skip quietly; it raises an error so the failure is visible.

## Key idea
No `mode()` means `errorifexists`: a rerun on the same path fails instead of appending, overwriting or skipping.
Q011674:
## What ignore means
`ignore` is the "create if not exists" save mode. If data is already present at the target, the writer neither fails nor changes anything; the DataFrame is simply not saved. If the target is empty or missing, the write happens as usual.
## When to use it
It fits one-time seeding of a reference dataset, where reruns must be harmless. It is a poor fit for incremental loads, because new rows are dropped without any message.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Exception:** raising an exception on existing data is the `errorifexists` mode. Ignore was chosen here exactly so that the call succeeds silently.
- ✓ **B. Ignore skips the write (correct):** because `/out/ref` already has data, Spark leaves the 100 existing rows as they are and discards the 500 new ones, so the count stays 100.
- ✗ **C. Append result:** adding rows to existing data is `mode("append")`. Ignore never touches the existing data, so no rows are added.
- ✗ **D. Overwrite result:** replacing the data with the new rows is `mode("overwrite")`. Ignore never deletes anything, so the old rows are not replaced.

## Key idea
`ignore` = write only if nothing is there yet; otherwise do nothing and report no error.
Q011675:
## Append is not idempotent
`append` adds new files next to the old ones. Spark does not compare rows, and a plain file source has no primary key or transaction log that recognizes a repeated batch. Running the same write twice therefore stores the data twice.
## Consequences for retries
- Retrying an `append` job after it already finished duplicates data.
- To make reruns safe, overwrite a deterministic location (for example one folder per batch date), or deduplicate on a key when reading.
- Transactional table formats can add idempotent writes; with plain files you design it yourself.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Append twice (correct):** two successful runs add two sets of files, so the 3 rows are stored twice and the read returns 6.
- ✗ **B. Skipping:** skipping an existing output belongs to `mode("ignore")`. Append writes new files whenever it is called.
- ✗ **C. Row merging:** Spark does not deduplicate on append and never compares new rows with stored rows, so identical rows are kept.
- ✗ **D. Invalidated path:** no such state exists for a file path. Readers simply see all part files that are present.

## Key idea
`append` is not idempotent: a retried successful write doubles the rows unless you deduplicate or overwrite a fixed location.
Q011676:
## Save modes are not transactions
The Spark guide states two warnings about save modes: they "do not utilize any locking and are not atomic", and when performing an `Overwrite`, "the data will be deleted before writing out the new data".
## What that means for a plain file path
- A crash between the delete and the end of the write leaves no complete old copy and no complete new copy.
- Readers that run at the same time can see missing or partial data.
- Safer patterns: write to a new, dated location and switch readers to it afterwards, or use a table format with transactions (such as Delta) so a failed write leaves the last committed version intact.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Rollback from a log:** plain Parquet paths have no transaction log. Only transactional table formats provide that, not the generic `overwrite` mode on files.
- ✗ **B. Atomic swap:** a temporary-directory swap would make overwrite atomic, which the guide says it is not. Writing happens at the target path.
- ✗ **C. Hidden backup:** Spark creates no backup copy of overwritten data. Once deleted, the old files are not recoverable through Spark.
- ✓ **D. Delete first, no atomicity (correct):** Spark clears the target before writing, so a failure halfway through can leave the previous night's data missing or the output partial, and the documented behavior gives no rollback.

## Key idea
Overwrite on a file path is delete-then-write, not atomic and not locked; a mid-write failure can lose the old data.
Q011677:
## Static and dynamic partition overwrite
For a partitioned data source, `spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode` controls what an overwrite deletes:
- `STATIC` (the default): Spark deletes the matching target before writing, which for a plain `overwrite` with `partitionBy` means every existing partition.
- `dynamic`: Spark does not delete ahead of time and overwrites only the partitions that receive data at runtime.
The setting can also be passed as a writer option, `partitionOverwriteMode`, and the option takes precedence over the session setting.
## Why not other modes
`append` and `ignore` change what happens to existing data in the whole target; neither means "replace the partitions I have data for".

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Ignore:** ignore skips the whole write because the path already has data, so tonight's day would never be written.
- ✗ **B. Append:** append adds files to dt=2024-01-03 beside the old ones instead of replacing them, so a rerun would double that day.
- ✓ **C. Dynamic mode (correct):** with `partitionOverwriteMode=dynamic` only dt=2024-01-03 is rewritten and the other days stay, because Spark overwrites just the partitions that hold rows in the DataFrame.
- ✗ **D. coalesce(1):** reducing the number of write tasks changes file counts, not which directories are deleted. In static mode the delete still happens first.

## Key idea
Replace only the partitions you have data for with `partitionOverwriteMode=dynamic`; static overwrite removes all of them.
Q011678:
## Default options apply
When you query `csv.`path``, Spark reads the file with the CSV source's default options. The `header` option defaults to `false`, so the first line is a data row and the columns are named `_c0`, `_c1`, ... with string type.
## How to get proper names
- Read with options: `spark.read.option("header", True).csv(path)` (optionally with `inferSchema` or an explicit schema), then register a temporary view if you want SQL.
- Or keep the direct query and select `_c0`, `_c1`, accepting the header as a row. That is rarely what you want.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Directories only:** a single file path is accepted. The path can also be a directory or a glob; that is not the reason for the error.
- ✓ **B. Defaults only (correct):** the header option is false by default, so `id` and `name` are not column names; Spark exposes `_c0` and `_c1`, and the unresolved `id` raises the exception.
- ✗ **C. View required:** direct file queries need no view. The same statement works, but with default-named columns.
- ✗ **D. Case sensitivity:** Spark SQL resolves column names case-insensitively by default, and the problem is that no column called `id` exists at all.

## Key idea
SQL on a CSV file uses default reader options (no header), so columns are `_c0`, `_c1`; use `spark.read.option("header", True)` to get real names.
Q011679:
## The text source schema
The `text` data source reads each line of every file as one row with a single string column called `value`. When partition directories are present, partition columns are added to it. Everything the other sources infer (types, headers, field names) does not exist for text, so you parse `value` yourself with `split`, `regexp_extract` or `from_json`.
## Contrast with CSV
CSV direct queries expose `_c0`, `_c1`, ...; JSON exposes the field names found in the data. Text always exposes `value`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. _c0:** `_c0` is the first column name produced by the CSV source with no header; the text source does not use positional names.
- ✗ **B. text:** the source name is not a column name. The query would fail with an unresolved column.
- ✗ **C. line:** no column called `line` exists for the text source, so the query fails to resolve it.
- ✓ **D. The value column (correct):** `text.` returns lines in a single string column named `value`, so filtering on `value LIKE '%ERROR%'` and counting rows gives the number of matching lines.

## Key idea
Reading text files gives one string column named `value` per line.
Q011680:
## Valid save mode names
The writer accepts exactly the save modes in the Spark guide:
- `error` or `errorifexists` (default)
- `append`
- `overwrite`
- `ignore`
Any other string is rejected with an error that lists the accepted modes. Spark does not guess intent from a near-synonym.
## Useful habit
Pass the mode as a string from this list, or in Scala/Java use the `SaveMode` enum, so that typos fail early rather than changing behavior.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Unknown mode name (correct):** replace is not in the list of save modes, so Spark rejects it with an error instead of mapping it to overwrite.
- ✗ **B. Mixed behavior:** no mode behaves as "append when exists, plain write otherwise" other than the append mode itself, and replace is not recognized.
- ✗ **C. Aliases:** the only alternative spellings are `error` for `errorifexists`; there is no alias like replace for overwrite.
- ✗ **D. Silent fallback:** Spark does not fall back to the default for an unrecognized name; a misspelled mode is an error.

## Key idea
Only error/errorifexists, append, overwrite and ignore are valid; other strings raise an error.
Q011681:
## The text writer is single column
The `text` source reads each line as one string column named `value`, and writes in the mirror image: the DataFrame must have exactly one column of string type, and each row becomes one line. A DataFrame with two columns is rejected before anything is written.
## Ways to write several fields
- Build one string column (`concat_ws(",", "id", "msg")`) and write it as text. You then own quoting and escaping.
- Use `csv` or `json` writers, which handle several columns, headers and quoting.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Drop the second column:** Spark does not silently truncate columns; the writer rejects the schema, and the save mode does not affect schema checks.
- ✗ **B. Tab separation and mkdir:** the text writer never joins columns with tabs, and Spark creates output directories itself, so the missing folder is not the problem.
- ✓ **C. Single string column only (correct):** the text writer cannot represent two columns, so the analysis fails; concatenating into one string column or choosing CSV/JSON solves it.
- ✗ **D. header option:** `header` is a CSV option. The text source has no header concept.

## Key idea
`write.text` needs exactly one string column; join columns into one or use csv/json.
Q011682:
## Reading and writing the same path
DataFrames are lazy: `spark.read.parquet(path)` does not read data until an action runs, and the write is that action. Overwrite deletes the target before writing, so the reader would find its own input deleted.
In practice the analyzer refuses this plan with an `AnalysisException` along the lines of "Cannot overwrite a path that is also being read from" (the Spark SQL guide does not list this check; it only warns that overwrite deletes data first). For plain files, write to a new path (or a staging path) and switch consumers after the job succeeds.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Memory buffering:** Spark does not hold the whole result in memory in order to delete its own input; output is produced by distributed tasks reading the files.
- ✗ **B. Empty result:** Spark's analysis step catches the conflict first, so the job fails instead of finishing with an empty dataset.
- ✗ **C. Filter pushdown:** pushdown limits which row groups are read, not which files overwrite deletes. Overwrite removes the whole target path.
- ✓ **D. Self overwrite is refused (correct):** the query both reads and overwrites `/out/orders`, so Spark rejects it before data is lost instead of reading from files it just deleted.

## Key idea
You cannot overwrite a file path you are lazily reading from: write elsewhere, then switch.
Q011683:
## saveAsTable versus a temporary view
- `saveAsTable("name")` writes the DataFrame's data to files (under the warehouse directory unless a `path` option is given) and creates a table entry in the metastore. It survives application restarts as long as the same metastore is used, and it can be read again with `spark.table("name")`.
- `createOrReplaceTempView("name")` registers a name for the DataFrame's query plan in the current session only. No data is written, and the name disappears when the session ends.
No Hive installation is needed: by default Spark creates a local metastore.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Neither survives:** tables created by `saveAsTable` are persistent, which is the point of the call; session-only lifetime applies to temporary views.
- ✓ **B. Persistent table (correct):** t2 has real files and a metastore entry, so it remains after the first application ends; the temporary view t1 was only a session-scoped name.
- ✗ **C. Both survive:** a temporary view is never written to the metastore, so it cannot be found by another application.
- ✗ **D. Only the view:** this reverses the behavior. The view holds a plan inside session memory, and the table is the object that persists.

## Key idea
`saveAsTable` = data plus metastore entry that outlives the session; a temp view = a session-scoped name for a plan.
Q011684:
## Bucketing needs a table
The guide says that for file-based data sources "bucketing and sorting are applicable only to persistent tables". The bucket count and columns are stored as table metadata in the metastore; later queries use that metadata to avoid shuffles. A plain path write has no place to keep it, so `save`-style methods (`parquet(path)`, `save(path)`) reject `bucketBy`.
## Correct form
```
df.write.bucketBy(8, "user_id").sortBy("user_id").saveAsTable("users")
```
`sortBy` is optional and sorts rows within each bucket. It can be used only together with `bucketBy`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Persistent tables only (correct):** bucketBy requires `saveAsTable`, so a path-based Parquet write is rejected with an AnalysisException.
- ✗ **B. Bucket files per partition:** a bucketed table does hold bucket files, but Spark creates them only through `saveAsTable`.
- ✗ **C. Silent ignore:** Spark does not drop a layout request quietly; it raises an error because the metadata could not be stored.
- ✗ **D. sortBy requirement:** the dependency runs the other way. `sortBy` needs `bucketBy`, while `bucketBy` works alone with a table.

## Key idea
`bucketBy` (and `sortBy`) work only with `saveAsTable`; path writes raise an error.
Q011685:
## Bucketing and joins
A bucketed table stores rows in a fixed number of files chosen by a hash of the bucket column. If two tables use the same bucket column (the join key) and the same bucket count, then rows with equal keys are already in matching buckets. Spark can join bucket i with bucket i and skip the shuffle that would otherwise be inserted as an `Exchange` before a sort-merge join.
- The setting `spark.sql.sources.bucketing.enabled` is `true` by default; when it is `false`, bucketed tables are treated as normal tables.
- Sorting within buckets (`sortBy`) can also save the local sort.
- Check the result with `df.explain()`: no `Exchange hashpartitioning(cust_id)` below the join.
## Why mention the broadcast threshold
Setting it to -1 turns off automatic broadcast joins, so the plan shows a sort-merge join and the benefit of bucketing is visible.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Broadcast:** the threshold is -1, so no automatic broadcast happens, and the threshold has nothing to do with bucketing.
- ✗ **B. Half shuffle:** when both sides are compatibly bucketed no side needs a shuffle; a one-sided shuffle occurs only if just one table is bucketed.
- ✓ **C. Co-bucketed join (correct):** both tables share the join key and bucket count 16, so Spark reads matching buckets together and the plan has a sort-merge join with no shuffle for either side.
- ✗ **D. Always shuffles:** that is the unbucketed behavior. Bucket metadata is used for joins and aggregations on the bucket columns precisely to avoid the shuffle.

## Key idea
Same bucket column and count on both tables = shuffle-free sort-merge join.
Q011686:
## Partitioning versus bucketing
- `partitionBy(col)` writes one directory per distinct value (`device_id=123/`). It gives partition pruning for filters on that column, but the directory count equals the number of distinct values. The guide notes it "has limited applicability to columns with high cardinality".
- `bucketBy(n, col)` hashes the column into a fixed number `n` of buckets. It "can be used when the number of unique values is unbounded", and helps joins and aggregations on that column.
## Rule of thumb
Partition on low-cardinality columns that queries filter on (date, country). Bucket on high-cardinality keys used for joins or lookups (user id, device id).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Too many directories (correct):** partitionBy on 50 million values makes millions of small directories and files, which overloads listing and the metastore; bucketBy gives a fixed layout for a column with unbounded values.
- ✗ **B. One file per device:** each directory holds at least one small file, but the cost of listing and tracking millions of them outweighs the pruning benefit.
- ✗ **C. 200 partitions:** the shuffle partition setting concerns shuffles, not the output directory layout. partitionBy writes a directory per value.
- ✗ **D. String only:** numeric, date and timestamp columns can be partition columns, and automatic type inference exists for them.

## Key idea
Partition by low-cardinality filter columns; bucket by high-cardinality key columns.
Q011687:
## Hive-style partition directories
`partitionBy` creates one directory level per column, in the order the columns are listed, and each level is named `column=value`. Example layout:
```
/out/s/country=KR/year=2025/part-00000-....parquet
/out/s/country=KR/year=2026/...
/out/s/country=US/year=2025/...
```
The column order matters for the layout: put the column most often used in filters first, and the one with the fewest distinct values at the top to avoid too many directories at the first level.
## Why this format
All built-in file sources can discover these `name=value` directories and infer the partition columns when they read the root path.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Plain nesting:** without `column=` prefixes the partition values could not be recovered by partition discovery.
- ✗ **B. Alphabetical order:** Spark uses the order in which you list the columns, not alphabetical order.
- ✗ **C. Single folder name:** each partition column gets its own directory level; Spark does not combine them with underscores.
- ✓ **D. Order and name=value (correct):** partitionBy("country","year") produces `country=KR` first and `year=2025` under it, which readers use to rebuild both columns.

## Key idea
`partitionBy(a, b)` writes `a=<v>/b=<v>/` folders in the listed order.
Q011688:
## Partition discovery
When Spark reads the root of a partitioned dataset it parses the `column=value` directory names, adds those columns to the schema (after the columns stored in the files) and uses them for pruning.
- Numeric, date, timestamp and string partition values get their types inferred automatically. For example `year=2025` becomes an integer.
- `spark.sql.sources.partitionColumnTypeInference.enabled` (default `true`) can be turned off, and then all partition columns are strings.
So no information is lost by `partitionBy`: the values are stored in the folder names instead of in the files.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. First and all strings:** partition columns are appended after the data columns, and numeric values are inferred as numeric types by default.
- ✓ **B. Discovered columns (correct):** Spark reads `country=KR/year=2025` names, adds country as string and year as an integer at the end of the schema, and the files stay smaller.
- ✗ **C. Dropped for good:** the values live in the directory names and come back on a read of the root path.
- ✗ **D. mergeSchema:** `mergeSchema` merges differing Parquet file schemas. Partition discovery is a separate, always-on feature.

## Key idea
Read the root path of a partitioned dataset and `name=value` folders come back as extra columns, with inferred types.
Q011689:
## Where discovery starts
Since Spark 1.6, partition discovery finds partitions only under the paths you pass. If you point at `/out/s/country=KR`, the `country=KR` part is above the starting point, so it is not a partition column.
- To keep it, set `basePath` in the reader options: `spark.read.option("basePath", "/out/s/").parquet("/out/s/country=KR")`.
- Alternatively read the root and filter on `country`; partition pruning then reads only that folder.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. basePath (correct):** it declares the table root, so the `country=KR` folder is treated as a partition level and the column is added to the result.
- ✗ **B. Constant column:** the column is not added because the starting path is below the partition level, so there is nothing to look for in the code.
- ✗ **C. Underscore names:** the only recognized form is `name=value`; renaming would break discovery.
- ✗ **D. mergeSchema:** this merges schemas found in Parquet files; the partition value comes from the path and not from the file schema.

## Key idea
Reading a single partition folder drops the partition column unless `basePath` points to the table root.
Q011690:
## Managed and external tables
- Without a `path` option, `saveAsTable` writes under the warehouse directory. This is a managed table, and dropping it removes the table's default path too.
- With `df.write.option("path", "/some/path").saveAsTable("t")`, the data lives at a location you choose. When the table is dropped, "the custom table path will not be removed and the table data is still there".
This matters when other jobs share the files, or when you want accidental drops not to destroy data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Trash folder:** Spark has no recycle bin for table files. A dropped table's files are either removed (default path) or left as they are (custom path), never moved aside.
- ✓ **B. External table (correct):** with a custom path, Spark keeps the files at `/lake/ext/sales` and drops only the metadata, so the data can be reattached to a new table.
- ✗ **C. Always delete:** only the default warehouse path is deleted on drop; custom paths are kept.
- ✗ **D. Unreadable:** the metastore stores only table metadata; the files remain ordinary Parquet files that a new table or reader can use.

## Key idea
`option("path", ...)` makes the table external: DROP TABLE leaves the files.
Q011691:
## Partition metadata in the metastore
Persistent datasource tables keep per-partition metadata in the metastore, so queries fetch only the needed partitions instead of listing all folders. The guide notes: "partition information is not gathered by default when creating external datasource tables (those with a `path` option). To sync the partition information in the metastore, you can invoke `MSCK REPAIR TABLE`."
## What the other commands do
- `ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE STATISTICS` records size and row-count statistics for the optimizer; it does not discover partitions.
- Clearing the cache drops cached data, not metastore partition entries.
- `partitionOverwriteMode` changes how an overwrite treats partitions when writing.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. ANALYZE:** statistics help planning and are separate from partition registration, so the new folder is still unknown.
- ✗ **B. partitionOverwriteMode:** this setting applies to overwrite writes; the table is only being read here.
- ✓ **C. MSCK REPAIR TABLE (correct):** it scans the table location, finds the new `dt=` folders and registers them as partitions, after which the filter finds the data.
- ✗ **D. clearCache:** this evicts cached data and does not add partitions to the metastore.

## Key idea
Partitions added to an external table behind Spark's back must be registered with `MSCK REPAIR TABLE`.
Q011692:
## insertInto is position based
`DataFrameWriter.insertInto(table)` writes into an existing table and "ignores the column names and just uses position-based resolution", unlike `saveAsTable`, which resolves columns by name. Both columns here are strings, so no type error warns you: the first DataFrame column goes into the first table column.
## Safe habits
- Reorder before writing: `df.select("first", "last").write.insertInto("people")`.
- Or append through `saveAsTable` with `mode("append")`, which matches by name.
- Check the schema of the target with `spark.table("people").printSchema()` first.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Nulls:** nothing is unmatched; every DataFrame column maps to a table column by position.
- ✗ **B. Failure:** matching types at the same position are accepted, so Spark finds nothing to reject.
- ✗ **C. By name:** that is how saveAsTable behaves, not insertInto; the doc states names are ignored.
- ✓ **D. Positional insert (correct):** `last` (Kim) lands in the first table column and `first` (Ana) in the second, producing a swapped but valid row.

## Key idea
`insertInto` is positional, `saveAsTable` is by name; reorder columns before inserting.
Q011693:
## What a partition column buys you
Partition directories encode the value, so a filter on the partition column lets Spark skip all non-matching directories before opening any file. In `explain()` the scan shows `PartitionFilters: [dt = 2024-06-01]`.
A filter on an ordinary column such as `amount` cannot skip directories. Parquet statistics may let Spark skip row groups inside files (pushed filters), but the files of all partitions still need to be opened.
## Choosing the column
Partition by the column most queries filter on and that has a modest number of distinct values.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bucketing needed:** partition pruning needs only the partitioned layout; bucketing is a separate feature.
- ✓ **B. Pruning only on the partition column (correct):** the `dt` filter selects one directory; the `amount` filter is a data filter that is evaluated inside each file.
- ✗ **C. Index on every column:** Spark does not build indexes. Skipping works from directory names and file statistics.
- ✗ **D. Numeric ordering:** the filter on `amount` cannot choose folders. Sorting by `sortBy` applies to buckets and does not make folder-level decisions.

## Key idea
Filter on the partition column to prune directories; other filters only skip data inside files.
Q011694:
## createOrReplaceTempView versus createTempView
- `createOrReplaceTempView(name)` creates a session-scoped view, or replaces an existing view with the same name.
- `createTempView(name)` fails with a `TempTableAlreadyExistsException` (an AnalysisException) if the name already exists.
Replace semantics make re-running a notebook cell safe, which is why the "OrReplace" form is the usual choice.
## What the name points to
A temporary view is one name for one query plan. Registering the same name again swaps the plan; it does not combine them.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. First wins:** nothing keeps the first registration when the "replace" variant is used.
- ✗ **B. Name conflict:** that error belongs to `createTempView`. The replace variant is designed not to raise it.
- ✗ **C. Union of both:** a view holds a single plan; Spark never merges plans registered under one name.
- ✓ **D. Replace (correct):** the second call replaces the plan behind `t`, so the count is over `range(5)` and the result is 5.

## Key idea
`createOrReplaceTempView` swaps the plan behind a name; `createTempView` errors if it exists.
Q011695:
## Views are names for plans
`createOrReplaceTempView` registers a logical plan under a name. No data is computed or stored; each query that uses the view is planned together with the view's plan, so the scan, join and aggregation run again each time (lazy evaluation).
## Reuse results
- `df.cache()` / `df.persist(level)` keeps computed partitions in memory or on disk after the first action; queries on the view then use the cached data.
- `CACHE TABLE agg` in SQL does the same for the view's name.
- Write the result with `saveAsTable` if it must survive the session.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Plan only (correct):** the view recomputes the full lineage on each query, so caching the DataFrame (or the view) after one action lets the next queries read from the cache.
- ✗ **B. Automatic caching:** Spark never caches a view on its own; the cache must be requested.
- ✗ **C. Writing to the warehouse:** a temporary view does not write anything to storage; persisting data is done by `saveAsTable`.
- ✗ **D. Eager materialization:** that would make the view a table. Spark registers the plan lazily and runs nothing at registration.

## Key idea
A temp view is a lazy name for a plan: cache the DataFrame to avoid recomputing it per query.
Q011696:
## View scopes
- A regular temporary view (`createOrReplaceTempView`, `createTempView`) is scoped to the session that created it.
- A global temporary view is "shared among all sessions and keep[s] alive until the Spark application terminates". It lives in the system database `global_temp`, so you "must use the qualified name" such as `SELECT * FROM global_temp.view1`.
It still lasts only for the application. For a name that survives restarts, use a table (`saveAsTable`).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Name that sounds global:** the name `global_t` has no special meaning, and `createTempView` is still session scoped.
- ✗ **B. Unqualified name:** global temporary views are found only under `global_temp`; the bare name `t` is looked up in the session's own catalog.
- ✓ **C. Global view plus qualified name (correct):** `createGlobalTempView` makes the view visible to every session in the application, and `global_temp.t` is the required way to reference it.
- ✗ **D. Session view with global_temp:** a regular temp view does not live in `global_temp`, so the second session finds nothing.

## Key idea
Share a view across sessions with `createGlobalTempView` and query `global_temp.<name>`.
Q011697:
## SQL on a view
`spark.sql(...)` runs a SQL statement and returns a DataFrame; the temporary view `t` is just the DataFrame under another name. The usual SQL evaluation order applies: `WHERE` filters rows before grouping, `GROUP BY` forms groups, aggregates are computed, `HAVING` filters groups on aggregate results, `ORDER BY` sorts.
Here the groups are `a` with values 1 and 3 (sum 4) and `b` with value 2 (sum 2). Only `a` has a sum greater than 2. The sum of integers is a long, shown as `s=4`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. HAVING on the aggregate (correct):** group `a` sums to 4 and passes, group `b` sums to 2 and is removed, so one row `Row(k='a', s=4)` is printed.
- ✗ **B. HAVING ignored:** HAVING removes groups, so b with sum 2 does not appear.
- ✗ **C. Row count:** `sum(v)` adds the values (1 + 3 = 4), while `count(*)` would return the number of rows (2).
- ✗ **D. Reversed condition:** HAVING keeps rows where the condition is true, which means sums greater than 2.

## Key idea
SQL on a temp view evaluates GROUP BY, then HAVING on the aggregates; `spark.sql` returns a DataFrame.
Q011698:
## Dropping a temporary view
`spark.catalog.dropTempView(name)` removes the name from the session catalog and returns `True` if a view was dropped (`False` if none existed). It removes only the registration: the DataFrame object and the underlying data are unaffected, and the DataFrame keeps working.
Any SQL that still refers to the name fails at analysis time with an `AnalysisException` (table or view not found). `createOrReplaceTempView("t")` can register the DataFrame again.
## Related
If the view was cached by name, `dropTempView` also uncaches it. Global views use `spark.catalog.dropGlobalTempView`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cannot drop:** dropping is exactly what the catalog method is for, and it returns a boolean.
- ✓ **B. Name removed, DataFrame kept (correct):** the SQL cannot resolve `t` anymore, so it raises an AnalysisException, but `df` still holds its own plan and data source and can be used.
- ✗ **C. Data deleted:** a temporary view never owns data; it is a name for a plan, so nothing is deleted.
- ✗ **D. Visible until session end:** the call removes the view immediately.

## Key idea
`dropTempView` removes only the SQL name; the DataFrame survives and the SQL on the name fails.
Q011699:
## Two directions of conversion
Spark keeps three representations of a moment: a number of seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC (a Unix epoch value, `bigint`), a `timestamp`/`date` type, and a formatted string. Each conversion has its own function.
- `from_unixtime(seconds, fmt)` turns epoch seconds into a **string** in the session time zone (`spark.sql.session.timeZone`). The default format is `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss`.
- `unix_timestamp(string, fmt)` goes the other way: it parses a string and returns epoch seconds as a `bigint`.
- `to_date(string, fmt)` parses a string into a `date`. The format describes how the *input text* looks.
## Example
`F.from_unixtime("ts", "yyyy-MM-dd")` on `1767225600` returns the text `2025-12-31` when the session time zone is a few hours behind UTC, and `2026-01-01` when it is UTC. The pattern letters (`yyyy`, `MM`, `dd`) follow the Spark datetime patterns.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. to_date with a pattern:** the pattern describes how to parse a string. A number is not text in the form `yyyy-MM-dd`, so this does not read epoch seconds, and the result would be a `date`, not a string.
- ✗ **B. unix_timestamp:** this converts a string into epoch seconds, the opposite direction. Passing a number and a date pattern would not give a date string.
- ✗ **C. cast to date:** Spark does not cast an integral number to a `date`, so the plan is rejected, and even a successful cast would give a `date`, not the string the report needs.
- ✓ **D. from_unixtime (correct):** it takes epoch seconds, applies the given pattern in the session time zone and returns a string, which is exactly the requested date text.

## Key idea
Epoch seconds to a readable string is `from_unixtime`; string to epoch seconds is `unix_timestamp`.
Q011700:
## Numbering of weekdays in Spark
`dayofweek(col)` extracts the day of the week as an integer from 1 (Sunday) to 7 (Saturday). This is different from the ISO convention (Monday is 1) used by Python's `isoweekday()` and from the zero-based `weekday()` in Python.
- `dayofweek` accepts a date, a timestamp or a string that can be cast to one of them.
- `date_format(d, "E")` returns the name of the day (for example `Sun`), when the numeric value is not needed.
- `weekofyear` and `dayofyear` extract other components in the same way; `year`, `month` and `dayofmonth` exist as well.
## Example
For `2024-03-10` (Sunday) the result is `1`; for the following Monday, `2024-03-11`, it is `2`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Zero-based Monday:** this is the Python `datetime.weekday()` convention, which Spark does not follow.
- ✗ **B. Zero-based Sunday:** Spark's weekday extraction is one-based; no value `0` is ever returned by `dayofweek`.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** dayofweek counts from 1 for Sunday up to 7 for Saturday, so the Sunday 2024-03-10 returns 1.
- ✗ **D. ISO-style 7:** in the ISO week Sunday is day 7, but Spark's `dayofweek` is not ISO numbered; it starts the week on Sunday.

## Key idea
`dayofweek` runs 1 (Sunday) to 7 (Saturday); do not assume the ISO or the Python numbering.
Q011701:
## Which date function returns which type
Extracting, formatting and truncating are three different jobs and their results have different types.
- `date_format(col, pattern)` formats a date or timestamp into text, so it always returns a **string** (`2026-11`).
- `month`, `year`, `dayofmonth`, `hour` and similar extractors return an **integer**.
- `trunc(date, unit)` cuts a `date` down to the start of the year, quarter, month or week and returns a **date** (`2026-11-01`). `date_trunc(unit, timestamp)` does the same for a timestamp and returns a **timestamp** (`2026-11-01 00:00:00`).
## Why it matters
A string like `2026-11` sorts and groups correctly but cannot be used in date arithmetic; the date from `trunc` can be used in `datediff` or range filters.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. date_format as date:** a formatted value is text, not a date, even when the pattern looks like a date. Only `to_date` or `trunc` return a `date`.
- ✗ **B. date_format as timestamp:** the pattern letters only decide the text layout; the output is a string. `trunc` returns a date, not a string.
